scenes.vo: Since Stuxnet, some of the most serious cyberattacks have targeted industrial controllers directly.
If yours were changed tonight, would anyone notice?
Controller settings are rarely compared against a trusted, known-good copy.

text.headline: Settings are rarely compared to a *trusted copy.*
text.status: last checked against trusted copy: never

scenes.vo: Every vendor has its own proprietary software. Licenses cost thousands, and those tools weren't designed for cybersecurity.

text.headline: A different *proprietary app* for every vendor
text.securitySub: built to configure, not to check

scenes.vo: What if checking your controllers was simple?
Introducing PEAT, the Process Extraction and Analysis Tool, created at Sandia National Laboratories.
PEAT finds the controllers on your network, and identifies each one.

text.title: Find and *identify* every controller
text.sub: Discovers devices on your network and confirms what they are.

scenes.vo: It gathers their logic, settings, logs, and firmware, over Ethernet or serial.

text.title: Gather what *matters*
text.sub: Logic, settings, logs and firmware, in one pass.

scenes.vo: Then it translates every vendor's format into one consistent view.

text.title: One *consistent view*
text.sub: Every vendor's format, translated into the same structure.

scenes.vo: Compare today's data with your trusted copy, or send it to tools like Elastic and Splunk.

text.title: See *what changed*
text.sub: Compare against your trusted copy, or send it to your SIEM.

scenes.vo: And it's designed with safety in mind. PEAT identifies each device carefully before collecting anything, and it's built to be gentle on sensitive equipment.

text.headline: Gentle on *sensitive equipment*
items: Works through devices one at a time

scenes.vo: It works with PLCs, protection relays, RTUs, and more, from over ten vendors.

text.headline: Equipment from *10+ vendors*
text.footer: 25+ device families · Ethernet & serial · project files too

scenes.vo: PEAT itself runs on Linux, Windows, macOS, or Docker, and it's easy to download and use.
Developers can use PEAT as a Python library, and build it into their own tools.

text.title: A *Python library*, too
text.sub: Build PEAT into your own scripts and tools.

scenes.vo: And it's modular, so adding support for a new device is straightforward.

text.title: Adding devices is *straightforward*
text.sub: Each device is its own module, written as one Python class.

scenes.vo: Best of all, PEAT is free. Open source, under GPL version three.
Start seeing your controllers clearly. Get PEAT on GitHub.
